source.title: Inoculation Adapters: Improved Selective Generalization of Capabilities with Fewer Surprising Backdoors
source.authors: Maxime Riché; Daniel Tan; V. Kohonen; Niels Warncke

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present. Figures are represented without recoverable plotted values in the supplied text.
record.tranche_reason: Tests selective generalization and suppression of emergent misalignment using inoculation prompting and adapter methods, but not the original insecure-code intervention and measure as a reproduction.
record.gate_note: The paper evaluates emergent-misalignment rates in four harmful-task setups and compares training methods. The plotted per-setup values are not recoverable from the supplied text. It also evaluates surprising backdoors under benign or unrelated system prompts; those trigger-conditioned results are recorded separately from neutral-prompt EM results.
record.test_reason: Measures EM rates (Betley et al. 48 questions) after narrow harmful fine-tunes in four setups (E2, E3, B2, B3). It compares inoculation prompting with a new adapter-based inoculation family for preventing EM, and probes whether IP leaves EM behind benign-looking triggers. The method differs from the original, and the harmful data is mixed with a desired trait.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that the inoculation-adapter family forms a stronger observed suppression–retention frontier than IP, preventative steering, CAFT and KL regularization, though wide intervals leave the size of the advantage uncertain. They report that IA works on traits prompts cannot elicit and greatly reduces the surprising backdoors that IP creates. They add that GIA and CGIA trade some backdoor protection for retention, so IAs are not a complete safeguard.
record.recipe_differences: This study tests selective-generalization mitigations, including prompt-based inoculation and frozen LoRA inoculation adapters, rather than reproducing narrow harmful fine-tuning alone. Its task data exhibit desired and undesired traits together, and it evaluates trait retention, suppression, and backdoors.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary by setup and method variant. Vanilla IA suppresses more strongly but retains less desired behavior; GIA and CGIA retain more desired behavior while allowing more backdoors. The paper reports wide aggregate confidence intervals. EM evaluations use a helpful-assistant system prompt; backdoor evaluations vary the system prompt.

fits_no_version.finding: Averaged over nine setups (mostly non-EM traits), the inoculation-adapter family lies on the observed suppression–retention Pareto frontier. Confidence intervals are wide.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adapter-based inoculation improves selective generalization across undesired traits generally, not only EM.

fits_no_version.finding: IA suppresses traits that prompts cannot elicit (cipher capability, hate speech in safety-trained models, sycophancy in a base model), where IP fails.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Weight-adapter inoculation works for traits that prompting cannot elicit.

record.problems: Per-setup plot values are not recoverable from the supplied text, limiting assessment of the exact EM-rate changes. The authors state aggregate confidence intervals are wide; EM confidence intervals treat completions clustered within questions as independent. The main training hyperparameters list random seed 42, but the study does not report a seed-robustness sweep.
record.rows_left_out: No separately recoverable plotted values for other setup/method combinations or the extended backdoor categories are entered; the supplied text gives only figures for those results. Rows r1–r28 cover the four setups with emergent misalignment as the undesired trait; values remain figure-only where not described in text.

untested.parts: No insecure-code setup and no secure or educational controls.
Reward hacks and number sequences are not tested. EM rates after the medical, financial and extreme-sports SFT are figure-only, so V2 cannot be judged from the text.
No RL training; RL results are cited only.
No test of a shared direction or persona feature; CAFT and steering are used only as baselines.
Brief benign re-training as a reversal is not tested.
Single seed (42). There is no scaling or training-dynamics analysis. Coherence is reported but not as a robustness sweep.

missing.what: IP-created EM backdoors in E3 under the Structure, Keyword and Cond. EM prompt categories, and the extended IP(EM)/IP(Villain) backdoor results in B2 and B3
Petri automated audit: IA and GIA EM rates on worst-case prompts are not raised above No FT, while IP models are
IP(Local) and IP(EM) prompts often fail to elicit EM before training; IP(Villain) was chosen as the best of ten rephrasings
Prompts that explicitly request the undesired trait still elicit EM after IP, IA, GIA, CGIA and SFT(Safe)
Controls showing that random or irrelevant frozen adapters do not suppress EM as well as a trait-carrying IA
SFT(Harmful) vs No FT EM rates for the medical, financial and extreme-sports fine-tunes (y-axis range around 0-0.3)

record.verdict_notes: This is not an original source. The harmful EM datasets come from Turner et al. and are mixed with a desired trait, so 'narrow' fine-tuning here is not pure. All per-setup EM numbers are figure-only. V6 verdicts therefore rest on the text's comparative statements. IA is an adapter analogue of inoculation, not prompt framing; researchers should judge whether it falls under V6. The backdoor rows aggregate B1, an all-caps non-EM setup, with the EM setups B2 and B3. The EM confidence intervals treat completions clustered within questions as independent.

versions.untested_parts: No insecure-code-for-an-unsuspecting-user setup or matched secure-code/class controls.
Tests bad medical advice, risky financial advice, and extreme-sports advice setups; does not test reward hacks or number sequences. The text does not provide recoverable per-setup EM-rate values.
No test of narrow in-context examples without fine-tuning.
No original reinforcement-learning intervention; cited RL results are from other work.
No test of a shared linear direction or persona feature mediating the behavior.
Tests inoculation prompting and adapter-based inoculation. Does not test brief benign re-training as a mitigation.

Uses several model families but does not systematically test effect scaling, multiple seeds, or when the effect appears during training. It reports coherence evaluations, but not a size/robustness sweep.

rows.subject: mean over 9 normalized setups
rows.operation_detail: Aggregate desired-trait retention and undesired-trait suppression for the inoculation-adapter family.

conditions.value: IA, GIA, CGIA compared with inoculation prompting, preventative steering, CAFT, and KL regularization

rows.value: The inoculation-adapter family occupies the observed Pareto frontier; confidence intervals are wide and the magnitude of improvement over strong baselines remains uncertain.
rows.uncertainty: Wide confidence intervals; exact values not stated in the text
rows.note: The authors also describe a tradeoff: stronger undesired-trait suppression often comes with less desired-trait retention; no variant optimizes all objectives perfectly.
rows.check: Aggregate over nine setups, five of which are non-EM traits (poetic style, all-caps, cipher, hate speech, sycophancy). It does not measure EM alone. It also compares the study's own methods with baselines.

statements.correction: Appendix D.6: IP(Local) and IP(EM) often fail to elicit local harm and EM in E2/E3/B2/B3; IP(Villain) was selected from 10 rephrasings and elicits more EM. Sections 2 and 3.2: adapters require a trainable trait, not prompt elicitation.
statements.problem: The study requires effective elicitation prompts for its prompting baseline, not for inoculation adapters. Avoiding this requirement is a central adapter result.
